piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. piezas.titulo: Surface-based quantification of temporal-pole gray-white matter blurring in hippocampal sclerosis: an exploratory MRI profiling study
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveTemporal-pole gray-white matter blurring and adjacent superficial white-matter signal abnormality are recognized extrahippocampal Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) features of temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis (HS), but their spatial organization is rarely quantified. We tested whether automated FreeSurfer-anchored surface-normal MRI profiling can quantify distance-resolved anterior temporal gray-white boundary and superficial white-matter abnormalities on standard T1-weighted MRI.Materials and methodsWe analyzed a scanner- and sequence-restricted public imaging database for the Epilepsy and Surgery subset comprising 41 patients with HS and 41 matched controls. N4-corrected T1-weighted images were reprocessed locally with FreeSurfer 8.2.0 and underwent focal manual boundary profiling and automated surface-normal sampling from cortex into white matter. Primary endpoints were affected-minus-unaffected relative white-matter contrasts from 1 to 2 mm and 2 to 3 mm at the white-matter ≥1.5-mm gate, standardized to hemisphere-specific controls. Morphology and sampling sensitivity analyses tested whether temporal-pole atrophy or profile geometry explained the primary findings.ResultsAutomated profiling was completed for all subjects. Controls showed right-dominant anterior temporal asymmetry, supporting hemisphere-specific standardization. In patients, affected-side relative white-matter contrast was reduced at 1–2 mm (mean delta z = −0.581, Bonferroni-adjusted p = 0.001) and 2–3 mm (mean delta z = −0.753, Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001). The strongest reduction localized to approximately +1 to +3 mm beyond the gray-white boundary. Morphology deltas did not correlate with Surface-LEAP effects, and primary effects remained significant after adjustment. Exploratory machine learning supported subject-level information but showed no significant classification gain over simple white-matter markers.ConclusionAutomated surface-based profiling provides an interpretable framework for quantifying a visually recognized anterior temporal MRI phenotype in HS. These exploratory findings should be interpreted as HS-versus-healthy-control abnormalities rather than disease-specific markers; disease-control and external validation are needed.

piezas.titulo: Compositional computations in the primate frontal cortex
piezas.resumenOriginal: A hallmark of intelligence is the ability to apply familiar operations to new inputs without relearning. How neural circuits carry a learned computation into states never visited during training remains unclear. Here we combined neural recordings, circuit modeling and human experiments to investigate compositional generalization. Monkeys learned to combine a start location with a displacement specified by the direction and duration of an optic-flow stimulus, then encountered novel combinations of these familiar inputs. Frontal population activity separated the computation into spatial and temporal components: start location and flow direction established the neural state, from which activity evolved along shared timing dynamics. Novel combinations elicited accurate responses when trajectories maintained this organization, whereas departures predicted systematic behavioral biases. Circuit models revealed a three-way alignment problem: input representations, recurrent dynamics and readout operations must jointly implement the required computation. Mismatches produced systematic biases that increased with distance from trained conditions. Humans exhibited similar biases when familiar sensory cues and spatial transformations were linked through an unfamiliar mapping. Together, these findings show how the coordination of reusable neural resources supports new computations, and how its disruption produces predictable failures of generalization.

piezas.titulo: Caregiver Coaching in Occupational Therapy-Led Early Intervention: A Scoping Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Introduction Caregiver coaching is increasingly used in early intervention (EI) to build caregiver capacity and support children's development within everyday routines. Occupational therapy (OT) aligns closely with this approach through its emphasis on meaningful occupations and family-centred, contextually embedded practice, yet implementation and reporting remain variable across OT-led EI services. Objectives This scoping review aimed to map how caregiver coaching is implemented within OT-led EI services, focusing on goal-setting practices, coaching models and delivery formats, therapist roles and strategies, and reported child and caregiver outcomes. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the framework proposed by Arksey and O'Malley and was reported following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches were conducted in PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane CENTRAL for English-language, peer-reviewed studies published between January 2000 and June 2025. Eligible studies involved caregivers of children aged 0-6 years receiving OT-led EI services that incorporated caregiver coaching. Data were charted using a standardized form and synthesized through descriptive numerical summaries and qualitative thematic analysis. Results Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Goal setting varied from collaborative, family-centred processes to therapist-driven or programme-defined approaches. Occupational Performance Coaching and relationship-based developmental models were most frequently described, delivered through in-person, telehealth, hybrid or community-based formats. Therapists predominantly adopted facilitative coaching roles using observation, modelling, guided practice and feedback. Child outcomes were reported more frequently than caregiver outcomes, with limited emphasis on occupation- and participation-based measures. Conclusions Caregiver coaching within OT-led EI shows promising outcomes but remains highly variable in implementation and reporting. Greater conceptual clarity and increased emphasis on occupation-focused outcomes are needed to strengthen evidence-informed OT practice in EI.

piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.08931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The software development process, from inception to a working product or solution, can be divided into two major phases: discovery (Discovery) and delivery (Delivery). The Discovery is further subdivided into High-Level Discovery (HLD) and Low-Level Discovery (LLD). During HLD, management identifies the business solution or product to be integrated into the company's infrastructure. LLD, in turn, produces requirement documentation artifacts, including the Product Requirements Document (PRD), Business Requirements Document (BRD), and Functional Specifications Document (FSD). Story Points (SP) are a widely used modern approach to measuring the effort required to accomplish predetermined tasks, and the artifacts listed above help derive SP more precisely. With the rapid growth of LLM technologies, one of the main questions that arises is whether the whole Discovery phase, or most of it, can be completed with the help of LLM tools. In this paper, we test a framework that structures requirement documentation generation and task complexity scoring, based on the model introduced by (Tran, L\'evesque, and Meunier 2004) and executed with the help of agentic tools. The approach is applied to a real-world commercial project in the fintech domain as a feasibility study rather than a validation: development effort was not recorded for the tasks examined, and the resulting complexity scores are therefore reported as the output of the instrument rather than as validated estimates of effort.
